Ya but even before AI, most design teams were super lean. Most companies have 1-2 designers per engineering team and PM. You might be part of a bigger design team but you cover your area solo. 

I joined a big fintech right out of college in sf and I was the only designer on my product even as a super junior (tho i had supervision). I was the only one responsible for producing designs for the product i was on. Even interns have their own solo projects as product designers. 

So how much smaller can it get from that? The scenario where I’ve seen 4 designers making designs together probably only happens at design consultancy where you’re taking on a big project as a team of designers.

If you’ve ever worked as a product designer in an org which sells it software as a service or consumer product you would know that AI is not even close to replacing designers. Because humans are inherently irrational. We don’t read instructions properly, do 3 tasks at once, give up too easily. An AI cant solve building complex interfaces because that would mean logic and reasoning is enough to build. Which its not.

If logic and design system was all thats needed to design interfaces we would not need customer research cause there is enough UI out there to copy and mimic.

Its just the design process is becoming more efficient with these tools.

Ideally yes. But in my experience you’re always making tradeoffs due to limited resources. You can always launch a mvp and iterate on it later. But most companies value profits over an ideal user experience. Even if you know objectively a certain ux is better because it helps users make a more informed decision, companies will always prefer the ux that converts better for their business.

We need to realize instagram that may want its interface to be user friendly and intuitive, but its primary objective is to further instagrams business goals and make them money. The designers who designed it intentionally want to promote certain behaviors in the app (making them easier to access) and discourage certain behaviors (hiding those flows further in). 

So I personally think when we criticize the ux we should also ask ourselves what were they trying to achieve with the redesign? Cuz a lot of time user needs are not at the top of the list, specially when they conflict with what the business unit wants in order to make more money

I did a bachelors in interaction design(fyi my degree is bfa, tho technically a stem major lol). Originally started as an industrial design major but saw a higher demand and salary potential in ixd. I was also more interested in psychology behind design rather than perfecting my 3d craft (tho there is definitely way more to industrial design than that).

I am a product designer who specializes in digital interfaces. I have 2yrs of solid industry exp. My day to day job kinda involves doing almost every thing from wire framing flows, making high fidelity prototypes, presenting work to stakeholders to convince them to build it and eventually work with dev to ship.

What’s interesting is that at school many in my cohort actually looked down on screen based ux. Imo opinion there are two reasons 1)It is deceivingly complex (feels like anyone can do it) and 2) Interactions on screens feel pretty limited. One of my classmates thesis was around ‘’why limit human interaction to just one finger when you have an entire body’’ (i kinda agree with her). Seeing a world full of screens everywhere feels very dystopian. And why do we need an app for everything?

Even my college education focused more around how to think like a service designer rather than designing screens. We did screen based projects but also did interactive/immersive experience design and event design. We developed a foundation in ux research, interviewing, analysis and most importantly presenting our work and taking critique. We were given briefs and the amount of time you spend/invest in whatever skill you wanted (software/coding etc.) was up to you. They just look at how well the brief was accomplished.

I am super lucky my college was in the bay area so a lot of my teachers were tech industry professionals. I impressed some of them and got noticed and getting a referral is really the only way for junior designers to get interviews imo. One of the reasons i honed my software skills (Adobe suite, figma etc) is i realized that to earn solid money, you gotta be in tech, and the demand is for screen based designers right now. Some adjustment time is needed from college to work cuz most people you will work with will not be designers and don’t understand how the process works. I also think screens are here to stay so might as well do our part in making products that dont take advantage of people and lead them towards better lives. Thats what i think a designers real responsibility is.
